answers_by_date.basis: In force: Constitution art. 14 bis ('igual remuneración por igual tarea', for every worker); LCT 20.744 arts. 17 (no discrimination by 'nacionalidad') and 81 (equal treatment); Ley 22.439 arts. 26-27 (permanent and temporary residents work 'gozando de la protección de las leyes que rigen la materia'). Art. 109 of Ley 22.439 let the employer off its labour obligations where a worker lawful at hiring later became irregular. Practice: CERD 2001 records that undocumented immigrants from neighbouring countries were vulnerable in the economic crisis. There is no wage-specific evidence.

Ley 25.871 (in force 21 Jan 2004) replaced Ley 22.439. Its art. 6 (equal access to rights in 'trabajo, empleo'), art. 16 and art. 56 (labour obligations owed 'cualquiera sea su condición migratoria') removed the art. 109 carve-out. Constitution art. 14 bis and LCT arts. 17 and 81 were unchanged. Practice evidence for 2004-05 is thin: CERD 2004 mainly welcomes the new law.

Same provisions; Decreto 616/2010 (May 2010) came after this date. Practice: CMW 2011 (covering the late 2000s) found that irregular migrant workers often received 'inadequate pay' and worked excessive hours in textiles, agriculture and domestic work. No pattern of wage discrimination against formally employed regular migrants was documented.

Same provisions (Ley 25.871 arts. 6, 16, 56; Decreto 616/2010 art. 56 on free legal aid; LCT arts. 17, 81; Constitution art. 14 bis). DNU 70/2017 came later and did not touch these articles. The practice evidence is the CMW 2011 findings and CELS's 2019 report on the CMW review (textile workers). Evidence for 2015 itself is thin.

The LCT's amendment list shows arts. 17 and 81 unchanged. Practice evidence on wages is indirect for 2000-2005 and thin for 2015.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2023 citation names the ICRMW as approved by 'Act 26.602'. Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(a) cites Ley 26.202 as the approving law; the ICRMW only applies from 2007. The 'Yes' itself holds.
answers.notes: The answer rests on statutes, not rulings. Through 2020, the equal-pay guarantee for regular workers rests on Constitution art. 14 bis and LCT arts. 17 and 81, all in force before 2000. The 2004 change widened protection for irregular workers (art. 56 replaced 22.439 art. 109).

answers_by_date.answer: Employment is tied to specific employer; change of employer possible, but requires new work permit application
answers_by_date.basis: Under Ley 22.439 and Reglamento 1434/87 as amended by Decreto 1023/94, the labour route to temporary residence was 'trabajador contratado'. Art. 15(e) as replaced by Decreto 1117/98 required a written contract with an employer established in the country, and the DNM resolved each application on the basis of that contract. Temporary residents could work only during the authorised stay (22.439 art. 27). Ley 24.493 reserved work to nationals and to foreigners authorised by migration law. There was no nationality-based (Mercosur) residence. Practice: CERD 2001 found residence papers costly and procedures 'lengthy and excessively bureaucratic'.

answers_by_date.answer: Employment is tied to specific employer; change of employer possible, but requires new work permit application
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 25.871 (from 21 Jan 2004) art. 23(a) created the 'trabajador migrante' subcategory: up to 3 years, 'con permiso para trabajar bajo relación de dependencia'. Art. 23(l) gave residence on nationality grounds to Mercosur, Chilean and Bolivian nationals, with no employer tie. The law had no regulation; art. 124 kept Decreto 1023/94 valid in the meantime. Practice evidence for 2004-05 is thin.

answers.sourcing_note: I could not open the text of Decreto 1434/87 and Decreto 1023/94: argentina.gob.ar has no text page, and the ACNUR copy returned 403. The 2000 regime is rebuilt from Decreto 1117/98, which replaced art. 15(e), and from Ley 22.439. Practice evidence for 2005 and 2015 is thin.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Neither Ley 25.871 art. 23(a) nor Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(a), which I read, expressly ties the 'trabajador migrante' permit to an employer or requires a new permit to change employer; any tie comes from DNM practice and requirements. Most migrants hold art. 23(l) nationality residence with free choice of employment, so the 2020 answer may understate the protection. The 2023 citation also gives the ICRMW as 'Act 26.602'; the approving law is Ley 26.202.
answers.notes: The option stays the same across all dates, but the regime changed: in 2000, labour residence depended on a written contract with a specific employer and no nationality route existed. From 2004, art. 23(l) (Mercosur nationality) gave most regional migrants residence free of any employer tie. This is why the change is coded 'not the same'.

answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439 art. 26: permanent residents may carry out any paid activity. Art. 27: temporary residents may do so 'por cuenta propia o en relación de dependencia' during their stay. Neither requires separate permission. Decreto 1117/98 shows that primary family members of permanent or temporary residents could apply for admission, but the derived-residence rule in Decreto 1434/87 art. 15 could not be read. Practice: CERD 2001 found residence papers costly and procedures bureaucratic.

Ley 25.871 art. 22: spouses of Argentines are permanent residents. Art. 51: permanent residents may do any work, and temporary residents may work during their stay, with no separate permit. Until regulation, Decreto 1023/94 stayed valid (art. 124). No practice evidence specific to spouses.
Same provisions; Decreto 616/2010 (May 2010) came after this date. No documented pattern of spouses being refused work.

Decreto 616/2010 art. 22(a)-(b) gives permanent residence to spouses of Argentines and of permanent residents. The last paragraph of art. 23 gives temporary residence to spouses of temporary residents, and Ley 25.871 art. 51 lets them work. DNM Disposición 4880/2015 (from 1 Oct 2015) extended this to registered unions convivenciales; it came after this date. No adverse practice evidence.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, migrants have a right to the same employment conditions and protections
answers_by_date.basis: Constitution art. 14 bis (limited hours, paid rest and holidays, protection against arbitrary dismissal) applies to every worker. LCT art. 17 bars discrimination by nationality. Ley 22.439 arts. 26-27 let permit holders work 'gozando de la protección de las leyes que rigen la materia'. Practice: CERD 2001 notes the crisis hit immigrants from neighbouring countries hard. There is no direct evidence on employment conditions.

Practice: CERD 2001 found xenophobic attitudes towards immigrants from neighbouring countries, which had 'given rise, on occasion, to violent incidents'.
